clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant, relatively pure cerebellar ataxia caused by a heterozygous missense variant in EEF2 (eukaryotic translation elongation factor 2) on chromosome 19p13.3.
Fits the Harding autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxia type III pattern — a predominantly cerebellar syndrome with few extracerebellar signs.
Adult onset with slowly progressive gait ataxia, limb dysmetria and dysarthria.
Oculomotor findings include gaze-evoked nystagmus and irregular or saccadic (broken) smooth pursuit.
Originally described in a large North American family of Norwegian ancestry.
Imaging shows relatively isolated cerebellar cortical atrophy with preservation of the brainstem.
Because the phenotype overlaps other pure cerebellar subtypes, gene-specific or panel testing is required for diagnosis.
It is not a repeat-expansion disorder, so genetic anticipation is not expected.
reference.pathophysiology: SCA26 is caused by a heterozygous missense variant in EEF2, which encodes eukaryotic elongation factor 2 — a GTP-binding protein that catalyses the ribosomal translocation step of messenger RNA translation, advancing the ribosome along the transcript during the elongation phase of protein synthesis. The disease-associated substitution is thought to subtly impair the fidelity and efficiency of translational elongation, a stress to which cerebellar Purkinje neurons are particularly vulnerable, producing selective cerebellar cortical degeneration and a comparatively pure ataxic phenotype. The mechanism is a dominant germline effect and does not involve any nucleotide repeat.
additionalDifferentials: SCA6 (CACNA1A) — late-onset, largely pure cerebellar ataxia
SCA5 (SPTBN2) — dominant pure cerebellar ataxia, sometimes early onset
SCA11 (TTBK2) — relatively benign pure cerebellar ataxia
SCA14 (PRKCG) — slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia, occasionally with myoclonus
SCA15/16 (ITPR1) — very slowly progressive pure cerebellar ataxia
SCA31 (BEAN1 intronic repeat) — late-onset pure cerebellar ataxia
Acquired late-onset cerebellar ataxia (alcohol-related, coeliac, paraneoplastic, vitamin deficiency)
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain to confirm relatively isolated cerebellar atrophy
Structured oculomotor examination documenting nystagmus and pursuit abnormalities
Hereditary-ataxia gene panel or exome including EEF2
Dedicated repeat-expansion testing to exclude subtypes such as SCA6 and SCA31
Screen for acquired cerebellar causes, including coeliac and paraneoplastic serology and relevant vitamin levels
Family segregation analysis and genetic counselling
redFlags: Prominent non-cerebellar signs (pyramidal, extrapyramidal or sensory) pointing to a different subtype or diagnosis
Systemic features suggesting a paraneoplastic or metabolic cause
reference.prognosis: The disorder progresses slowly over many years to decades and tends to follow a relatively benign course compared with the multisystem ataxias, with independent ambulation often preserved for a prolonged period.
pitfalls: Labelling the patient as idiopathic late-onset cerebellar ataxia without pursuing genetic testing
Assuming a repeat-expansion mechanism and omitting sequencing-based analysis
Attributing the ataxia to alcohol or another acquired cause without reviewing the family history
Overlooking a positive family history when the phenotype is mild and slowly evolving
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: With no disease-modifying therapy for this EEF2-related ataxia, anchor care on physiotherapy for gait and balance, occupational therapy, and speech and language therapy for dysarthria
Institute falls prevention and provide mobility aids for progressive gait ataxia and limb dysmetria
Monitor for bulbar dysfunction with periodic swallow assessment as disease advances
Address visual symptoms from gaze-evoked nystagmus and broken smooth pursuit with ophthalmology or orthoptic input
Provide multidisciplinary ataxia clinic follow-up, reflecting the relatively benign, predominantly cerebellar course
Offer genetic counselling with cascade testing, noting this is a point-mutation disorder without anticipation
